entries.title: CPD issues alert after armed robberies at dating app meetups in Princeton Park
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are warning the public after three people were robbed at gunpoint in Princeton Park during meetings set up on dating apps, according to a bulletin released Wednesday.</p><p>The three reported robberies occurred in the 9200 block of South Harvard Avenue when someone was meeting another person from a dating app, and a man would demand their possessions at gunpoint, police said.</p><p>The most recent robberies occurred at 2:30 p.m. Oct. 18 and 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, police said. The suspect is described as a man about 6 feet tall with a slim build and light complexion who was wearing black clothing and a mask.</p><p>Anyone with information on the robberies can contact Chicago police at (312)747-8273.</p>

entries.title: Man critically injured in Chatham shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot multiple times in a shooting in the Chatham neighborhood Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 38, was in an alley near the 8100 block of South Drexel Avenue at 4:40 p.m. when he was shot in the arm, leg and torso, police said. He was taken to Trinity Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody. An investigation is ongoing, police said. </p>

entries.title: University of Chicago students rally with 'Jane Doe' in wake of sexual assault reports
entries.summary: <p>When Ray Epstein looked out into a crowd of more than 100 University of Chicago students near a fraternity house where a woman said she was sexually assaulted, a request was made. </p><p>Epstein, who represented the sexual assault prevention company What They Don't Say, asked them to raise their hands if they knew a survivor of sexual violence or had been a victim themselves. </p><p>Nearly every hand in the crowd went up. Some teared up or hugged another person.</p><p>On Wednesday night, the students gathered to call on the University of Chicago to improve its sexual assault prevention and survivor support<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/21/university-chicago-sexual-assault" target="_blank" > in the wake of two cases in recent weeks </a>tied to the campus.</p><p>“How many Jane Does will it take?” Epstein said. “How many Jane Does will it take before universities begin treating sexual violence as a problem worth preventing instead of one worth reacting to after the entries.title: Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson emitting young-Michael Jordan vibes with his play, talk
entries.summary: <p>It sounds like the good old days whenever he’s announced during introductions.</p><p>“From North Carolina …” Tim Sinclair blares.</p><p>Bulls fans of a certain age connect that school to one person, Michael Jordan. But in just a handful of games, Caleb Wilson has generated an excitement similar to the one those Bulls fans felt in 1984, when Jordan was just starting to get cooking on the West Side.</p><p>Not to put pressure on the kid — he’s 20 years old and looks younger — but the 16 points he scored in his first NBA game matched what His Airness scored in his. Five MVP Awards, 10 NBA scoring championships and six titles are right around the corner.</p><p>But here’s the thing: Wilson didn’t even give us the chance to anoint him as the Bulls’ next franchise player. He beat us to it, setting his sights on being the Rookie of the Year and striving to be the best player — ever.</p><p>Is there a rule against one city having two such players? Wilson would be happy to break it.</p><p>He doesn’t even think he’s putting undue pressure on himself. He believes he can do it.</p><p>“It’s just expectations for myself,” he said Wednesday. “If I stay healthy and I continue to do the work that I’m supposed to do, I feel like there’s no reason why I shouldn’t be a great player and hopefully Rookie of the Year.”</p><p>He certainly showed glimpses Monday in an otherwise forgettable night for the Bulls in Boston. During one stretch of the second quarter, Wilson beat Paul George one-on-one from the perimeter with a jab step and finished with a dunk, then beat George and Mitchell Robinson on the baseline with floater.</p><p>Those aren’t Wilson’s college contemporaries. Those are longtime NBA veterans. But Wilson has no symptoms of imposter syndrome.</p><p>“I definitely feel like I belong,” he said. “I feel like I’ve had great games, and, shoot, I’ve played against the best players and I’ve held my own and done well.”</p><p>That might look cocky in print, but it sounded nothing of the sort. When told that it appeared he was picking things up on the floor quickly, he responded with the most matter-of-fact “I told you so” ever spoken.</p><p>“Every game I learn something new, and I feel like every game I get better,” he said. “No matter what the stats say, I feel like I get better every single game. It’s so fun to see growth, and it’s so rapid for me.”</p><p>“We’re coaching him hard; he asked for that,” Bulls coach Tiago Splitter said. “He’s doing a lot of things that he’s not used to. He played at the four, big-man position in college, and he’s guarding [the Celtics’ Jayson] Tatum in a pick-and-roll. So there’s a lot of things for him to learn.”</p><p>One thing he already learned came from Jordan, who famously made up grudges and slights to motivate himself on the court. Wilson, a self-professed nice guy, said he needs to do something similar to conjure the venom required to compete in the NBA.</p><p>“When I go on the court, it’s hard to be, like, frustrated, but that’s when I play my best,” Wilson said. “So I just have to get that level of frustration and anger so I can play and be the best player I can be.”</p><p>MJ would be proud.</p><p>He also would be proud of the attention Wilson is drawing from the opposition. Wilson hasn’t even played a half-dozen games yet, but he appears to be at the top of scouting reports.</p><p>“Something that I’ve noticed, I’m usually getting the best defender every night,” Wilson said. “And I’m usually drawing two or three people every time I attack the paint. So just having that knowledge and knowing the gravity that I have in being able to create for others is something that I feel like I’ve really grown with lately.”</p><p>Wilson said his playmaking, not his scoring, has grown the fastest in his short time as a pro.</p><p>“I’ve missed a lot of shots I usually don’t miss lately,” he said. “It’s just conditioning, trying to adapt to the NBA game. But I’d say my playmaking is where I’m most happy that I’ve been growing offensively. Having that ability to make plays without turning the ball over is something that I’m really proud of. But I really hope that I can continue to grow there.”</p><p>Wilson already has faced some of the best players in the league, and more are on tap, including rematches with the Celtics and Knicks and his first look at LeBron James and the 76ers. He said sharing the court with such stars is surreal, which must be an understatement for a 20-year-old.</p><p>“I’m just a kid, so having an opportunity to play in Madison Square and TD Garden, that’s never going to not feel crazy to me,” Wilson said. “I’ve wanted to do that my whole life. So every time I go into an arena, I’m going to play to the best of my ability. I’m always going to do that.”</p><p>Sounds like a certain someone also from North Carolina.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Bulls offense is still a work in progress but ball security improving
entries.summary: <p>It’s been a point of emphasis since Tiago Splitter moved his stuff into the Bulls coaching office: Get Josh Giddey to play cleaner offense.</p><p>Last season, the veteran point guard handed out a career-high 9.1 assists per game but also established a career-high in turnovers with 3.6. His first year with the Bulls it was 2.9 turnovers per game. Coming from the Spurs culture like Splitter did, that’s a no-no.</p><p>So while the sample size is small so far, Giddey entered the game with the defending champions on Wednesday leading the team with 7.3 assists per game but just two turnovers per contest.</p><p>“Josh is also getting used to playing solo as bringing the ball (up),” Splitter said. “Before he had a lot of guys that can bring up the ball and create a bit more, but I think he’s doing a tremendous job of not turning the ball over as much. His assist-to-turnover ratio is way better. Yes, I want him to be more aggressive, yes, we’re not playing the way we want to yet. I think the process has been right.”</p><p>It may be right but not without problems.</p><p>The starters are still feeling each other out as far as shot selection and sharing the basketball, evident by the league-worst 40.6% shooting from the field and 23.8% from three-point range.</p><p>Numbers that Splitter feels will turn soon.</p><p>“Offensively, we’re getting the shots, most of the time, the shots we want,” Splitter said. “Unfortunately, we’re not making shots right now, which is part of the game. Sometimes you go through slumps, and we’ve got to start to make shots. But the process is right.”</p><p>Giddey was on the same page as his coach, feeling like it was just a matter of time.</p><p>“Every team coming out of training camp probably feels good about themselves, every team probably says they’re better than people think they’re going to be and blah, blah, blah,” Giddey said. “I believe in the group we have to start putting it together and we look good in stretches and we look horrible in stretches. So it’s just a matter of making those good stretches longer and those bad stretches shorter.”</p><p></p><p><b>Speed kills</b></p><p></p><p>Splitter was informed that almost 15% of the league was on the injury report before Wednesday’s games and did some self-scouting on how he would handle today’s style of play.</p><p>“I think the speed of the game is at a different level,” Splitter said. “If you want to ask me as a former player, the way I played was very slow, so I could not have played at this pace. Maybe as a back-up center. But yeah, the league is fast. Then you get to the games and the pressure, the high intensity is more than the summer, there’s an adjustment there, so you got to be careful how much you play your guys. If you’re not careful with the minutes and the loads, all that, it’s science like two plus two is four.”</p><p></p><p><b>Training room</b></p><p></p><p>The plan was to continue ramping up Nic Claxton (left hamstring) the next day and then take him on the East Coast swing to Boston, Philadelphia and New York. Does that mean the expected starting center will make his Bulls debut on that trip?</p><p>Not so fast.</p><p>“We’ll talk to our performance team, see where he’s at,” Splitter said. “He’s probably going to go with us because he’s almost there, just be part of what we’re doing as a group, even on the road. That’s the plan.”</p><p>As far as the two other injuries the group has been dealing with Patrick Williams (right adductor strain) and Tobe Awaka (left ankle sprain) remained out.</p>
